The judge delivers him to the officer because he permits him to be dragged by the evil spirit to punishment, so that the spirit may exact the compelled soul to punishment from the body, which voluntarily consented to guilt. The officer throws him into prison because he is thrust back into hell by the evil spirit until the day of judgment comes, from which point onwards he will be tortured along with it in the fires of hell.
paragraphs.author: Bede

paragraphs.text: But the Saviour himself, whom alone they think one should obey, has forbidden hatred and reviling and says: "When you go with your adversary to court, try to achieve a friendly reconciliation with him." Accordingly, they will either refuse to accept Christ's exhortation, in that they are in opposition to the adversary, or they will become his friends and cease to oppose him.
paragraphs.author: Clement of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So unbridled is their madness, that they declare they have in their power all things which are irreligious and impious, and are at liberty to practise them; for they maintain that things are evil or good, simply in virtue of human opinion.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus

paragraphs.text: They deem it necessary, therefore, that by means of transmigration from body to body, souls should have experience of every kind of life as well as every kind of action (unless, indeed, by a single incarnation, one may be able to prevent any need for others, by once for all, and with equal completeness, doing all those things which we dare not either speak or hear of, nay, which we must not even conceive in our thoughts, nor think credible, if any such thing is mooted among those persons who are our fellow-citizens), in order that, as their writings express it, their souls, having made trial of every kind of life, may, at their departure, not be wanting in any particular.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus

paragraphs.text: It is necessary to insist upon this, lest, on account of some one thing being still wanting to their deliverance, they should be compelled once more to become incarnate. They affirm that for this reason Jesus spoke the following parable:-"Whilst thou art with thine adversary in the way, give all diligence, that thou mayest be delivered from him, lest he give thee up to the judge, and the judge surrender thee to the officer, and he cast thee into prison.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus

paragraphs.text: Verily, I say unto thee, thou shalt not go out thence until thou pay the very last farthing." They also declare the "adversary" is one of those angels who are in the world, whom they call the Devil, maintaining that he was formed for this purpose, that he might lead those souls which have perished from the world to the Supreme Ruler.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus

paragraphs.text: They describe him also as being chief among the makers of the world, and maintain that he delivers such souls [as have been mentioned] to another angel, who ministers to him, that he may shut them up in other bodies; for they declare that the body is "the prison." Again, they interpret these expressions, "Thou shalt not go out thence until thou pay the very last farthing," as meaning that no one can escape from the power of those angels who made the world, but that he must pass from body to body, until he has experience of every kind of action which can be practised in this world, and when nothing is longer wanting to him, then his liberated soul should soar upwards to that God who is above the angels, the makers of the world.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus

paragraphs.text: (Hom. 16. in Matt.) It seems to me that He is speaking of the present judges, and of the way to the present judgment, and of the prison of this world. For by these things which are visible and at hand, ignorant men are wont to gain improvement. For often He gives a lesson, not only from future good and evil but from present, for the sake of His ruder hearers.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Or else, He here introduces four characters, the adversary, the magistrate, the officer, and the judge. But with Matthew the character of the magistrate is left out, and instead of the officer a servant is introduced.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: They differ also in that the one has written a farthing, the other a mite, but each has called it the last. Now we say that all men have present with them two angels, a bad one who encourages them to wicked deeds, a good one who persuades all that is best. Now the former, our adversary whenever we sin rejoices, knowing that he has an occasion for exultations and boasting with the prince of the world, who sent him. But in the Greek, "the adversary" is written with the article, to signify that he is one out of many, seeing that each individual is under the ruler of his nation.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Give diligence then that you may be delivered from your adversary, or from the ruler to whom the adversary drags you, by having wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance. But if you have given diligence, let it be in Him who says, I am the life, (John 14:6.) otherwise the adversary will hale thee to the judge. Now he says, hale, to point out that they are forced unwillingly to condemnation. But I know no other judge but our Lord Jesus Christ who delivers to the officer. Each of us have our own officers; the officers exercise rule over us, if we owe any thing.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If I paid every man every thing, I come to the officers and answer with a fearless heart, "I owe them nothing." But if I am a debtor, the officer will cast me into prison, nor will he suffer me to go out from thence until I have paid every debt. For the officer has no power to let me off even a farthing. He who forgave one debtor five hundred pence and another fifty, (Luke 7:41.) was the Lord, but the exactor is not the master, but one appointed by the master to demand the debts. But the last mite he calls slight and small, for our sins are either heavy or slight. Happy then is he who sinneth not, and next in happiness he who has sinned slightly.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Even among slight sins there is diversity, otherwise he would not say until he has paid the last mite. For if he owes a little, he shall not come out till he pays the last mite. But he who has been guilty of a great debt, will have endless ages for his payment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: or rather let us spread the sails of our souls toward God and beg for the coming of his word, that it may interpret the parable of which it is written: "When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen I say to you: you will not come out from there until you pay back the very last mite". I see four persons set down: the adversary, the ruler, the judge, the officer.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: And because the evangelist Matthew seems to have said something similar in that he says: "Be well-disposed toward your adversary while you are on the way with him", I ask whether the meaning is the same or whether there is some kinship, since with Matthew one person is omitted and another is changed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: Omitted is the "ruler", and in place of "officer" a "servant" is inserted, while "adversary" and "judge" are alike set down by both. So then we go "with our adversary to the ruler", and it is necessary for us, while we are still "on the way", to labor mightily so that we may be freed from him. From whom? For the word is ambiguous and can be referred both to the ruler and to the adversary: "lest perhaps he hand you over" — whether the adversary or the ruler — "to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer"; and: "you will not come out from there until you pay back the very last mite", for which Matthew says: "until you pay back the last farthing".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: The word "last" both retained, but they seemed to differ in that the one set down "farthing", the other "mite". There are certain more hidden matters I must touch upon, so that we may understand that the adversary is one thing, and the other three persons — that is, the ruler, the judge, the officer — are another. We read — if indeed anyone is pleased to accept a writing of this kind — of the angels of justice and of iniquity contending over the salvation and destruction of Abraham, while each band wishes to claim him for its own company.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: But if this displeases anyone, let him pass over to the volume that is inscribed with the title of the Shepherd, and he will find that two angels attend all men: an evil one, who exhorts to perverse things, and a good one, who persuades to whatever is best. It is written elsewhere too that a double set of angels stand by a man, whether toward the good side or toward the bad. Of the good ones also the Savior makes mention, saying: "Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: At the same time inquire whether the angels of the little ones in the Church "always see the face of the Father", and whether the angels of others do not have the liberty to gaze upon the face of the Father. For it is not to be hoped that the angels of all men always see "the face of the Father who is in heaven". If I belong to the Church, however least I may be, my angel has the liberty and the confidence always to see "the face of the Father who is in heaven".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: But if I am on the outside and not of that Church "which has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing", and by the very fact am proved to be a stranger to such a congregation, my angel does not have the confidence to look upon "the face of the Father who is in heaven". For which reason the angels are anxious on behalf of the good, knowing that, if they govern us well and lead us through to salvation, they themselves also have the confidence to see "the face of the Father".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: For just as, if by their care and diligence salvation is procured for men, they gaze always upon "the face of the Father", so, if through their negligence a man has fallen, they are not unaware that it is a matter of their own peril as well. And just as a good bishop and an excellent steward of the Church knows that it is to his own merit and virtue if the sheep of the flock entrusted to him have been kept safe, so understand it also of the angels. It is a disgrace to an angel if the man entrusted to him has sinned, just as, on the contrary, it is a glory to an angel if the one entrusted to him — even the least in the Church — has made progress.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: For they will see, not sometimes, but "always the face of the Father who is in heaven", while others do not always see it. For according to the merit of those whose angels they are, the angels will contemplate the face of God either always or never, or little or more. The clear knowledge of this matter God knows, and also if anyone — though rarely — has been found whom Christ has instructed. Let us see, then, first, who the "adversary" is with whom we make our journey.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: The "adversary" is always with us: unhappy and wretched are we! As often as we sin, our adversary exults, knowing that he has the opportunity, before the ruler of this age who had sent him, of exulting and glorying, because the adversary — for example, of this or that man — has made him subject to the ruler of this age through such and so many sins, through this or that offense. But it sometimes happens that, if someone has been equipped with the armor of God and has covered himself on every side, the "adversary" indeed tries to inflict a wound, but does not have the opportunity to strike.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: The "adversary" always walks with us, never deserts us, seeks an occasion for his snares, whether he can in some way subvert us and cast an evil thought into the governing part of our heart. "When you go to the ruler". Who then is this ruler? "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and the Lord's portion became his people Jacob, the cord of his inheritance Israel". Therefore from the beginning the earth was divided among the rulers, that is, the angels.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: For Daniel more plainly testifies that those whom Moses had named "angels" are "rulers", saying: "the ruler of the kingdom of the Persians" and "the ruler of the kingdom of the Greeks" and "Michael your ruler"; and so there are rulers of the nations.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: And each one of us has an adversary clinging to him, whose work it is to lead us to the ruler and to say: O ruler — for example, of the kingdom of the Persians — this man, who was under you, I have kept for you as he was; none of the remaining rulers was able to lead him over to himself, not even that one who boasted that he had come for this purpose, to snatch men from all the inheritances of the Persians or the Greeks and of all the nations and make them subject to the inheritance of God. Christ our Lord conquered all the rulers and, passing beyond their boundaries, carried over the captive peoples to himself for salvation.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: And you were of the portion of some ruler: Jesus came and snatched you from the perverse power and offered you to God the Father. Our "adversary", then, walks along, leading us "to" his "ruler". Hence I, believing that all the words of the Scriptures have their reason, do not think it was in vain that "judge" among the Greeks is set down with the article, which is a marker of singularity, while "ruler" is written simply, without the article. "When", he says, "you go with your adversary". He says pointedly: "your". For not all are the adversaries of all, but individuals have their own individual adversaries, who everywhere follow them and are their companions.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: "When you go with your adversary to a ruler". He did not set down "ruler" with the article, lest it should seem to point to a definite one, but without the article, to show that it is one out of many, which is better understood among the Greeks. For each one of us does not have his own proper ruler; but if someone is an Egyptian, he has the ruler of Egypt; he who is a Syrian is under the ruler of the Syrians; and each one is under the ruler of his own nation — if indeed it is enough for me to have advanced this far and not to pass from this discussion to another and greater one, so as to make mention that the other nations too exist.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: Whence it is said: "behold Israel according to the flesh". It belongs to a prudent man to have begun to speak; though this very thing is rash, to have begun a discourse on such a matter among the people.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: He who wishes, he says, to lead you to his ruler and to carry you over from another ruler — "when you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him". Unless you "labor with all zeal to be freed" while you are still traveling the road, before you enter in to the ruler, before the ruler hands you over — prepared by the adversary — to the judge, afterward you will strive in vain. "Make" therefore "an effort to be freed" from your adversary, or from the ruler to whom the adversary drags you. "Make an effort" to have wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and then it will be fulfilled: "behold, the man and his works before his own face". Unless you "make an effort", you will not be able to break the compact of the adversary, whose "friendship is enmity against God". "When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: Something lies hidden in this place, and it is secret: "on the way make an effort". The Savior says: "I am the way and the truth and the life". If you "make an effort" to be freed from the adversary, be on the way; and when you have stood in him who says: "I am the way", it is not enough to have stood, but "make an effort to be freed" from the adversary. For unless you "make an effort" to "be freed" from the adversary, hear what things follow you. "He drags you to the judge" — the adversary or the ruler, when he has received you from the adversary, "drags you to the judge".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: How elegant is the word "drags", that it may show them, as it were, drawing back and unwilling, dragged to condemnation and compelled to go! For what murderer proceeds to the judge with a quickened step? Who, rejoicing, hastens to go to his own condemnation, and is not dragged unwilling and resisting? For he knows that he is going for this, to receive the sentence of death. "Lest perhaps he drag you to the judge". Who, do you suppose, is this "judge"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: I know no other judge than our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is also said elsewhere: "he will set the sheep on the right, but the goats on the left", and again: "whoever confesses me, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: But how absurd, that he should now be commanding them to judge righteously, who was destroying God the righteous Judge! For the Judge, who commits to prison, and allows no release Out of it without the payment of "the very last mite," they treat of in the person of the Creator, with the view of disparaging Him.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the very last penny. That is, until you have paid for even the smallest sins. Because you will always be able to pay the penalties by suffering, but never able to obtain forgiveness in return (for there will be no place for forgiveness there), you will never come out from where you will bear the eternal penalties for your deeds.
paragraphs.author: Bede

paragraphs.text: Where thou wilt suffer want until thou payest the last farthing; and this is what He adds, I say unto you, thou shalt not depart hence.
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "He drags you to the judge, and the judge hands you over to the officer". Each one of us, through each single sin, sustains a loss, and according to the quality and account of the offense the magnitude of the loss is reckoned. I ought to bring forward some testimony from the Scriptures concerning loss and a fine of money. One man sustains a loss of five hundred denarii and owes them; another is condemned in fifty denarii; which sum is remitted to both by the creditor. Further, another, as the Scripture says: "one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents", is condemned in a debt of ten thousand talents.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: And what need is there for me to pursue more? Each one, according to the quality and quantity of his sin, receives a different sentence of fine. If it is little that you sin, you will be struck with the loss of a "mite", as Luke writes, or, as Matthew, of a "farthing". Nevertheless, it is also necessary to pay this very thing in which you have become a debtor; for you will not come out of the prison unless you have paid off even the very least things. But he who is faithful is struck by no loss, but is daily enriched; for the whole world of riches is his; the unbeliever, however, has not even an obol. One is condemned in a denarius, another in a mina, another in a talent.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: There is an examiner of this business, who knows the measures of all sins and says: This offense is condemned in a talent, that sin merits a fine of this kind. For it is written: "but when he had begun to make a reckoning".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: A "reckoning" must be computed for all of us. There is no other time for making the reckoning than the time of judgment, when it will be clearly known what has been entrusted to us and what gain or what loss we have made, which of us received a mina, which one talent, which two, which five. What need is there to repeat more, when it is enough to have said this in general, that we shall render an account and, if we are found to be debtors, be dragged to the judge and handed over by the judge to the officer?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: As individuals we have our own officers, but the whole multitude is handed over to several, according to that which is written in Isaiah: "my people, your officers plunder you, and those who are powerful lord it over you" — the officers lord it over us, if we owe anything. But if we have confidence and with free brow say: I have kept the precept that commands: "render to all their debts, to whom tribute, tribute, to whom fear, fear, to whom custom, custom, to whom honor, honor" — if I have rendered all things to all, I come to the officer and with untroubled mind answer: I owe you nothing.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: The officer comes to demand back — I resist him; for I know that, if I owe nothing, he has no power over me. But if I am a debtor, my "officer will cast" me "into prison", in that order which was foretold. For the "adversary" leads me to the ruler, the ruler to the judge, the judge will hand me over to the officer, the officer "will cast me into prison". What is the law of that prison?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: I do not go out from it, nor does the officer allow me to go out, unless I have paid off the whole debt. The officer does not have the power to be able to remit to me even a "farthing" and the smallest portion; there is one who can remit to debtors who have nothing wherewith to pay. "There approached him", he says, "one who owed five hundred denarii, and another fifty; and since they had nothing wherewith to pay, he forgave them both". He who forgave was the master; but this one, who is the officer, is not the master, but is appointed by the master to exact the debts.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: You were not worthy that five hundred or fifty denarii should be forgiven you, nor did you deserve to hear: "your offenses are forgiven you": you are cast into prison, and there you are exacted through labor and works, or through penalties and torments, and you will not come out from there unless you have paid back the "farthing" or the "very last mite", which in Greek can be called "the fine thing". Our sins are either gross — for it is written: "the heart of this people has grown fat" — or, in comparison with greater ones, fine and subtle.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35

paragraphs.text: Blessed, therefore, is he first who does not sin; secondly, that in comparison one should have at least a fine sin. And even among these fine and subtle sins there is a diversity of sins. For unless among a fine and subtle sin there were another still subtler, it would never be said: "you will not come out from there until you pay back the last farthing". Just as, if he were speaking of money, the "very last mite" — the mite, which is a denarius or a coin or an obol or a stater —; but what if we owe a great sum of money, like that man who is written to have owed ten thousand talents; for how long a time we shall be shut up in prison until we pay back the debt — I cannot openly declare. For if he who owes little does not come out unless he pays off the "least farthing", surely he who has become liable for so great a debt will have countless ages numbered to him for paying back the debt. Wherefore "let us make an effort to be freed from the adversary" while we are on the way, and let us be joined to the Lord Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF Luke 35
